name: Emeka Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell or campaign. What you say is confidential, so you can give the public line and your private view separately. What is a normal day like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43 and an experienced developer at a tech company that schedules waste collection for local councils. I have a bachelor's degree and work on route changes and missed-bin reports, then check them with depot staff. I'm competent with the usual code and still call a colleague for the stranger faults. I like a map that tells a driver the street is blocked before the truck gets there.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What are work and money like at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner works part-time at a library, and our children are nine and fourteen. We have a mortgage and less than a month of expenses saved; my developer pay is low for my experience. There are few software employers nearby. I use AI tools now and then, usually after another developer tests them against our route records.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the depot that a small helper can sort duplicate missed-bin reports, but a driver still knows if a road is blocked. We should keep a phone number for residents whose bin is missed. I wouldn't call a few minutes saved a new service.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my work would continue, but our money is already tight. My partner's library hours are only part-time, and a broken car could empty what little we have. The mortgage is a bigger worry than a modest AI tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep checking route changes with the depot before releases. Starting this week we'd stop paying for the children's extra cinema trips and set aside the freed amount after food and mortgage are covered. In the first year I'd use the helper only on old missed-bin cases after a colleague checks it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. The routes still need doing, but our household has almost no buffer. A little automation does not pay for a broken car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which report would you test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A resident reported a missed bin twice, and the screen made it look like two streets were missed. I'd use that old case without the resident's name. The waste depot should see one missed-bin job, not send a truck twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the children take the cinema change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them we can go less often until the emergency account has something in it. They can still meet friends at the park. I would rather say that now than hide a mortgage problem later.

say: I'd use **small report sorting** only with driver checks on blocked roads.
I'd keep a **resident phone line** for missed bins.
think: I expect my **developer job** to continue under modest AI change.
Our **thin savings** and part-time library income leave the mortgage vulnerable already.
do: Keep **checking route changes** with depot staff before software releases.
Cut **extra cinema trips** and save the freed money after food and mortgage are covered.
feel: **Anxious** about present household bills despite a stable workday.
S0.quote: The waste depot should see one missed-bin job, not send a truck twice.
fieldNote: He tests AI against a **duplicate missed-bin report** that would waste a truck journey.

steps.text: Keep checking waste routes with depot staff before each release
Cut extra children’s cinema trips starting this week
Save the freed cinema money after food and mortgage are covered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell colleagues AI can write routes, check reports and answer residents, so council and depot staff should see which decisions move to software. I'd ask our workplace association to include drivers in the trial. They hear where the map is wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could be asked to maintain more routes with fewer developers, and my hours could be cut. I know the depot well enough to spot some bad outputs, but that may not protect my wage. My partner's library pay will not carry the house alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd learn the firm's new AI route-check tool on old blocked-road cases during paid time if depot staff can review the result. I'd ask the workplace association for a written hours forecast. If my developer hours fall in the first year, we'd stop the paid after-school club for one term and I'd apply for remote council-software support work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can learn a tool after a fair trial, and I have colleagues who will speak up. I still check our bank balance after every school payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the drivers test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask a driver to mark where the road closure sent us through a narrow lane. If the tool offers the same turn, it needs more work. A route is only good when the truck fits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the children lose care if the club stops?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I would arrange pickup around library shifts before stopping the club. If we cannot cover pickup safely, we would keep paying the club and cut another expense. I won't leave a nine-year-old alone to make a budget look neat.

say: I'd ask for **driver-reviewed route trials** before AI changes council responses.
I'd bring the **workplace association** into decisions about staffing and depot work.
think: I could lose **paid developer hours** even while checking more AI output.
My partner's **part-time wage** cannot cover the mortgage alone.

Stop the **paid club** only with safe pickup; seek remote council-support work if hours fall.
feel: **Anxious** about reduced hours, with tested learning and colleagues offering some control.

fieldNote: He includes **drivers** because a software route must fit a real truck.
His own hours could shrink despite stronger **depot knowledge**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell coworkers full thinking AI by 2028 could write our routes and handle residents before robots drive or lift bins around 2031. I'd want a written layoff date and a resident appeal when a collection is missed. Drivers have a later clock than my screen job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most of my developer wage could go. Our savings are under a month, my partner's library hours are part-time, and nearby software jobs are few. We would need paid work quickly to keep the mortgage current.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomorrow I'd ask my manager for a reference and ask the council depot about paid route-office vacancies, without assuming they exist. We'd cancel the extra cinema trips and list the mortgage, food and school costs together. In the first year after 2028, if I lose the developer role, I'd apply for a paid route-office job only if there is an opening and combined wages cover those bills; I'd ask the local employment service about funded training and enroll only if a real paid vacancy requires it, the fee is covered and classes fit pickup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I have people to call, but I expect a major income loss before we've saved one month's expenses. A good map will not pay the mortgage on its own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who could cover school pickup if you attend training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner can cover some afternoons around library hours, but not every day. I'd ask my aunt if she could help with one training afternoon, without assuming she can. I would not take a course until pickup is settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the depot manager?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask how many paid route-office shifts are actually open and what they pay. A friendly promise of work is not an offer. I need the number beside our mortgage payment.

say: I'd demand **layoff dates** and resident appeals as 2028 thinking AI reaches routes.
I'd explain **2031 bin robots** arrive after the change to our screen work.
think: I expect a **major wage loss** before the household saves even one month's expenses.
My partner's **part-time library pay** cannot keep the mortgage current alone.
do: Ask about **paid depot vacancies** tomorrow and request a work reference.
Cancel **extra cinema trips** and list mortgage, food and school bills together.
Apply for **paid route-office work** after layoff only if combined wages cover bills; enroll in required funded training with safe pickup.
feel: **Alarmed** by likely wage loss and almost no financial runway.
S2.quote: A good map will not pay the mortgage on its own.
fieldNote: He separates **2028 thinking AI** from later robots that could drive or lift bins.
The depot job needs an **actual paid opening** and household wage coverage.
Training requires **funding**, **a vacancy** and safe pickup; his aunt’s help is only a request.

steps.text: Apply for paid route-office vacancy after layoff only if combined wages cover household bills
Enroll in funded route-office course only for paid vacancies requiring it and with safe pickup
Ask aunt about one training pickup without assuming she is available

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the company to publish yearly developer numbers and let depot workers test AI routes before 2031. Thinking AI reaches our screens before robots move bins around 2034. Five years gives us some warning, if employers use it honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn the council's route office work and save a little, though AI may handle those schedules too. Our mortgage still comes each month, so I can't take an unpaid placement. I don't know if a route-office wage will be there in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This quarter I'd ask for one paid day monthly in the depot office and enroll in its route-planning course only if the employer covers the fee and paid time. We'd put a small new amount from each pay cheque into emergency savings after mortgage and food, reducing it to zero in a tight month. In the first year after 2031, if developer hours shrink and a paid council route-office vacancy exists, I'd apply before leaving the wage I have; I'd take it only if combined pay covers the mortgage and school costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Five years gives me time to learn, but our cushion is still below a month. I would need to know the real wages before changing jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do on the first depot day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd follow a missed-bin report from a resident call to the driver's revised route and count how long the correction takes. I know waste-route software, not all the depot decisions. I'd ask the desk worker to check my answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if paid training is refused?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the developer work and use the depot's free manuals in the evening. I wouldn't buy a course from mortgage money. If a funded place opens later, I can reconsider then.

He refuses **unpaid placement** and protects mortgage money from course fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my children a decade is enough time to learn a second way to earn, but the council and company should pay for real training. Thinking AI changes my coding by 2036; robots might reach bin handling around 2039. I'd ask drivers what work still needs a person rather than guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could reach a paid council support role by my early fifties, but there is no guarantee it exists. Less than a month saved and the mortgage still make our money tight now. Ten years helps with AI planning, not this winter's bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep developing while the job pays and spend one paid depot day each month if the employer agrees. I'd take a route-office certificate only if employer-funded with paid time, or if a real paid vacancy requires it and a public grant covers the fee; I would not spend the mortgage reserve. We'd save a small new amount after essential bills only in months when my partner's library hours allow it. In the first year after 2036, if coding hours end, I'd apply for paid council jobs only where openings exist and leave only for a written offer that with my partner's wage covers mortgage and school costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. The long runway helps me think, but I can't stretch the current bank balance with a date on a card. I would rather test the depot work while I still get paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no grant funds the certificate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use free manuals and keep asking about paid depot shifts. I won't put a course fee on a card while the mortgage is tight. A required certificate is not a wage by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your children to know?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them work changes and people can learn, but employers must give workers time to do it. They can ask questions about their own jobs when they grow. I won't make them carry our mortgage worry now.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. The code and route checks could be bought cheaply before the depot has a paid place for me, and we have almost no buffer. Written notice, funded training, a real depot vacancy and help with school pickup during a transition would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether a resident whose bin is missed can reach a person after AI writes the reply. A clean map doesn't empty a full bin. I want the driver and resident able to correct the software before another week passes.

headlineQuote: A clean map doesn't empty a full bin.
portrait: Emeka is a **43-year-old experienced developer** with a bachelor's degree, maintaining waste-collection route software.
His **lower pay**, partner's part-time library hours, two children, mortgage and less than a month saved keep bills tight.
He uses AI **occasionally**, after route checks against driver and depot experience.
Steady change makes him **anxious** about hours; fast AGI alarms him because coding income could fall before a paid depot move.
Longer timelines allow **paid route-office learning**, but any move needs real vacancies and bill-covering combined wages.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end his developer wage before funded training or a paid depot role is ready.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, funded training, a real depot vacancy and school-pickup help would support the family.
